notes.headline: Applied Materials: revenue up 53% and earnings nearly doubled, with another record quarter guided
notes.takeaway: Revenue reached a record $10.41 billion, up 53%, and adjusted EPS of $4.16 beat the $4.05 consensus and was 92% above last year. Guidance for next quarter is $11.1 billion of revenue and $4.35 of EPS at the midpoint. The shares still fell after the report, a sign of how much was already expected.
results: Applied Materials reported revenue of $10.41 billion for its fiscal fourth quarter ended October 25, up 53% from a year earlier. Adjusted earnings per share were a record $4.16, up 92% and ahead of a consensus of about $4.05; reported EPS was $3.40, up 43%.

Adjusted gross margin was 50.6%, up 2.5 points on the year, and adjusted operating income was a record $3.68 billion, or 35.3% of revenue. Cash from operations was a record $3.30 billion in the quarter, and the company returned $2.42 billion to shareholders through $2.0 billion of buybacks and $421 million of dividends.

For the full fiscal year, revenue was a record $34.45 billion, up 21%, and adjusted EPS was $12.89, up 37%. The gap between the full-year growth of 21% and the fourth-quarter growth of 53% shows how sharply the business accelerated through the year.
mgmt: Chief executive Gary Dickerson said the company is on track to grow its Semiconductor Systems business by more than 40% in calendar 2026, and that AI continues to drive strong incremental demand for chips, leaving Applied positioned for what he called multi-year revenue and profit growth.
Chief financial officer Brice Hill pointed to technology leadership in the most critical areas of wafer fabrication equipment and to record quarterly free cash flow.

For the first quarter of fiscal 2027 Applied expects revenue of $11.1 billion, plus or minus $500 million, and adjusted EPS of $4.35, plus or minus $0.20. At the midpoint that is about 7% above the quarter just reported.
view: Semiconductor equipment is the most cyclical corner of the technology industry, and this is what the top of an upswing looks like in the numbers: revenue up by half, earnings nearly doubling, gross margin above 50% for a company that spent years in the mid-40s. Applied sells the machines that deposit and remove the layers of material on a chip, and every leading-edge logic chip, every high-bandwidth memory chip and every advanced package needs more of those steps than the generation before. AI has not just raised demand for chips; it has raised the equipment intensity of making them.

The operating leverage is the most impressive part. Revenue grew 53% and adjusted EPS grew 92%, because gross margin widened 2.5 points and operating costs grew far more slowly than sales. An equipment maker’s factory and research costs are largely fixed in the short run, so incremental revenue drops through at very high rates. The same arithmetic works in reverse in a downturn, which is the reason these companies have never held premium valuations for long.

That is the context for the shares falling on a record quarter and a guide above it. The guidance midpoint implies sequential growth of about 7% after a year in which quarterly revenue rose from under $8 billion to over $10 billion. Growth is continuing, but the rate of acceleration has peaked, and equipment stocks have historically topped when orders stop accelerating, well before revenue declines. Investors who own this stock for the cycle watch the second derivative.

The longer-term case is that this cycle is less fragile than previous ones. Demand is coming from several directions at once — leading-edge logic, advanced memory for AI servers, and advanced packaging — and governments are subsidising new fabs in the United States, Europe and Japan. Against that sit export restrictions on China, historically one of Applied’s largest markets, and the concentration of AI spending among a few customers whose budgets set the pace for the whole supply chain. Applied is an excellent business at the favourable point of its cycle; the price has to be judged with both halves of that sentence in mind.
notes.watch: Order growth and the gross margin in the January quarter. Margin holding above 50% while revenue grows says pricing power is intact; any commentary on customers delaying equipment deliveries would be the first sign of the cycle maturing.
